dek: Fury vs Joshua tickets up to £13,128 sold out instantly for the Dec 11 Cardiff fight.

slides.label: What happened
slides.text: Tickets for Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua at Cardiff's Principality Stadium *sold out in one hour*.

slides.label: The numbers
slides.text: Around *80,000 tickets* went on sale, priced from £88.50 up to £13,128 including fees.

slides.label: The demand
slides.text: Within minutes of the 12:00 BST sale, more than *500,000 fans* were stuck in the online queue.

slides.label: Resale chaos
slides.text: Ringside VIP seats quickly popped up on resale sites for as much as *£73,645*.

slides.label: Fight details
slides.text: The bill starts Dec 11, but Fury and Joshua aren't expected to fight until *01:00 GMT* on Dec 12.

slides.label: The near miss
slides.text: Just 11 days before the sale, a dispute over UFC boss Dana White's promotional role almost *killed the fight*.

slides.label: The money
slides.text: Fury and Joshua are reportedly sharing a purse worth close to *$200m*, streamed globally on Netflix.

slides.label: Why it matters
slides.text: Two British fighters just proved homegrown stars can out-earn and out-draw the biggest names in global sport.

caption_instagram:
Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua tickets for their December 11 fight at Cardiff's Principality Stadium sold out in just one hour, with prices ranging from £88.50 to £13,128, according to BBC Sport.

More than 500,000 fans were stuck in the online queue within minutes of the sale going live, and resale sites are already flipping ringside seats for £73,645. The all-British heavyweight showdown streams globally on Netflix, with ringwalks expected around 1am on December 12, after a dispute over UFC boss Dana White's promotional role almost derailed the whole event just 11 days before tickets dropped.

Fury and Joshua are reportedly sharing a purse close to $200m, proof that British boxing still carries massive global weight.

Would you pay £13,128 for ringside? Yes or no.

caption_linkedin:
Fury vs Joshua just showed what demand looks like when a market is starved for a product. Tickets priced up to £13,128 sold out in one hour, with over 500,000 people in the online queue within minutes, according to BBC Sport.

The backstory matters as much as the sellout. Just 11 days before tickets went live, the entire event was in jeopardy over a dispute about UFC chief Dana White's promotional role. Organizers resolved it, locked in Cardiff's Principality Stadium after Wembley and Madison Square Garden fell through, and still delivered a Netflix-streamed global event with a reported $200m purse split.

For founders and operators, the lesson isn't the price tag, it's the sequencing: resolve the structural conflict first, then let demand do the rest. Scarcity plus clarity moved 80,000 seats faster than almost any sports ticket sale in recent memory.
